sections.title: 1. Kinship & Family Structure
sections.content:
Kinship as the Core Social Unit

The Rigvedic society was structured fundamentally around kinship (blood relations) rather than territory. Social identity, security, and access to resources were entirely determined by lineage. The primary social unit was the patriarchal family, known as the Kula or Griha. The head of this household was the eldest male member, designated as the Kulapa or Grihapati, who wielded absolute authority over the family members and assets, though his power was tempered by customary ethics.

Hierarchical Social Divisions

The social structure ascended from the family unit to larger kinship divisions:

  • Kula / Griha: The fundamental family unit headed by the Kulapa.
  • Grama: A cluster of families or a mobile kin-camp. In battle and pastoral migrations, the Grama functioned as a cohesive unit led by the Gramani.
  • Vis: A subdivision of the tribe (clan canton), headed by the Vispati, representing a collection of Gramas.
  • Jana: The entire tribe or ethnic assembly (e.g., Bharatas, Purus), headed by the Rajan.

Joint Family System and Patrilineality

The family was of a joint nature, often spanning three generations living together under one roof. Patrilineal descent was strictly observed; sons were highly desired (referred to as Viras) to secure the lineage, inherit family herds, and perform ancestral rites. Despite the strong patriarchal bias, the family unit operated as a cooperative economic unit where tasks were divided based on age and gender.

sections.title: 2. Social Stratification & Varna System
sections.content:
From Egalitarianism to Stratification

The early Rigvedic society was largely egalitarian, with no rigid class divisions. The primary social distinction was between the incoming Indo-Aryans (Aryas) and the indigenous populations (referred to as Dasas and Dasyus). This distinction was initially based on language, religious practices, and physical traits (referred to as Varna, meaning color or outward appearance).

The Concept of Varna

In the early Rig Vedic period, Varna did not denote a hereditary caste system. Instead, it was a flexible division based on occupations and social standing. The society was divided broadly into three functional groups:

  1. Priests (Brahmanas): Handled sacrifices and sacred chants.
  2. Warriors (Rajanyas/Kshatriyas): Protected the clan and led military expeditions.
  3. Commoners (Vis/Vaishyas): Engaged in pastoralism, trade, and agriculture.

An individual's Varna was fluid; a hymn in Mandala 9 famously records a poet saying: 'I am a singer, my father is a physician, my mother grinds corn with stone...', highlighting the lack of occupational rigidity.

The Purusha Sukta and Later Stratification

Towards the end of the Rigvedic period, specifically in the Purusha Sukta hymn of the 10th Mandala (a later addition), the four-fold Varna system is mentioned for the first time. It describes the creation of the four varnas from the body of the primeval giant, Purusha: Brahmanas from the mouth, Rajanyas from the arms, Vaishyas from the thighs, and Shudras from the feet. This laid the theoretical foundation for the rigid social hierarchy that characterized the Later Vedic period.

sections.title: 3. Position of Women
sections.content:
High Status and Public Participation

Women in early Vedic society occupied a highly respectable position. They were not confined to the domestic sphere and had access to education and political assemblies. Women actively participated in tribal assemblies like the Sabha and Vidatha. The term Sabhāvati is used to describe a woman eligible to participate in assembly discussions.

Access to Education and Rituals

Women were initiated into education through the Upanayana ceremony (sacred thread investiture) and studied the Vedas. Several women scholars composed Vedic hymns and were designated as Brahmavadinis (lifelong students of sacred lore). Prominent examples include:

  • Lopamudra: Wife of sage Agastya, who composed hymns in Mandala 1.
  • Ghosha: Composed hymns dedicated to the Ashvins in Mandala 10.
  • Apala, Vishvavara, and Sikata: Celebrated women seers who sponsored and performed sacrifices.

Marriage and Social Norms

Marriage was considered a sacred, cooperative partnership. Key aspects of Rigvedic marriage include:

  • Consent and Age: Child marriage was absent; girls married after reaching maturity. Instances of choice in choosing partners (swayamvara-like) are recorded.
  • Niyoga (Levirate): The practice of Niyoga was allowed, where a childless widow could cohabit with her brother-in-law to produce an heir.
  • Widow Remarriage: Widows had the right to remarry, and the custom of Sati (widow burning) was completely absent.
  • Patriarchal Limits: Despite these freedoms, women did not have independent property rights (inheritance went to sons), and the birth of a son was celebrated far more than a daughter.

sections.title: 4. Pastoral-Agricultural Economy & Material Culture
sections.content:
Cattle as the Measure of Wealth

The Rigvedic economy was predominantly pastoral, with agriculture playing a secondary role. The cow (Gau) was the central unit of economic value, acting as a currency and a measure of wealth. Wealthy individuals were called Gomat (possessor of cattle). Wars were primarily fought to capture cattle, and the terms for conflict (e.g., Gavisthi, Gaveshana) literally mean 'search for cows'. The cow was declared Aghnya (not to be killed) in several hymns, indicating its sacred and economic sanctity.

Vedic Diet and Beverages

The diet consisted primarily of milk and milk products (ghee, butter, curd), and barley (Yava), which was the chief grain cultivated. Meat was consumed occasionally during sacrifices. Two sacred beverages are highlighted:

  • Soma: A sacred, intoxicating drink prepared from a plant found in the mountains (Mujavant). It was offered to the gods, especially Indra, and consumed during rituals.
  • Sura: A secular, popular liquor brewed from grain, though often disapproved of by priests due to its intoxicating effects.

Clothing, Ornaments, and Entertainment

The dress of the Vedic people was simple, consisting of two or three pieces of cloth: the Nivi (undergarment), the Vasa (garment), and the Atka or Adhivasa (cloak/overgarment). Both men and women wore ornaments made of gold (Niska and Rukma) and beads. Popular forms of entertainment included chariot racing, dicing (playing with Aksa), music (flutes, lutes, drums), and dancing.

sections.title: 5. Daily Life, Education & Professional Castes
sections.content:
The Oral Tradition and Gurukula

Education was entirely oral and focused on the transmission of sacred hymns and rituals. The teacher (Guru) recited the hymns, and the students repeated them with precise pronunciation and pitch. The system of education was centered in the household of the teacher, representing the early prototype of the Gurukula system. There was a strong emphasis on moral conduct, discipline, and the preservation of cosmic order (Rta).

Artisans and Craftsmen

The Rigvedic economy was supported by skilled professional groups who enjoyed respectable social status. Unlike the Later Vedic and classical periods, artisans were not marginalized. Key groups mentioned include:

  • Takshan (Carpenter): Crafted spoked-wheel chariots (Ratha) which were vital for war and migrations.
  • Karmara (Metalworker): Worked with copper and bronze (referred to as Ayas) to make tools and weapons.
  • Vayatri (Weaver): Primarily women, who spun and wove wool and cotton garments.
  • Charmakara (Leatherworker): Prepared leather for reins, bowstrings, and water bags.

Hospitality and Social Ethics

Hospitality was a supreme moral virtue. Guests were treated with deep respect, and terms like Atithi reflect their honor. A wealthy host who slaughtered a cow or ox for an honored guest was referred to as Goghna. Charity (Dana) and sharing resources with clansmen were highly valued behaviors, ensuring social harmony in the tribe.

sections.title: 6. Social Transition & Class Differentiation
sections.content:
Transition to Sedentary Agriculture

Towards the end of the Rigvedic period (around 1000 BCE), the Aryan clans began migrating eastward from the Sapta-Sindhu region (Punjab) towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab. This migration coincided with a transition from a nomadic pastoral lifestyle to settled agriculture. Land, which was previously a communal pasture, began to acquire territorial significance, and individual claims on cultivated plots (known as Kshetra) started to emerge.

Emergence of Social Inequality

As settled agriculture generated surpluses, social inequality increased. Chieftains (Rajans) and priests (Brahmanas) accumulated greater wealth, particularly in the form of cattle, horses, and captive women. The common people (Vis) were increasingly pressured to provide voluntary gifts (Bali), which slowly began to resemble mandatory tributes. This created a clear class division between the ruling/priestly elites and the working peasantry.

Interaction with Indigenous Populations

The expansion into new territories led to greater interaction and assimilation with the indigenous populations (Dasas and Dasyus). Many defeated indigenous people were incorporated into the Aryan social fold at the bottom of the hierarchy as agricultural laborers and domestic servants. This social integration of non-Aryan groups culminated in the creation of the fourth Varna, the Shudras, establishing the institutionalized four-fold hierarchy of Later Vedic times.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the 'Varna' system in the Rigvedic period:
1. The early Rigvedic period was characterized by a highly rigid, birth-based class system.
2. The concept of Varna originally denoted color or physical appearance.
3. The four-fold division of society is mentioned for the first time in the Purusha Sukta of the 10th Mandala.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. The early Rigvedic class divisions were fluid and occupational, not rigid or hereditary, making Statement 1 false.

2. Women were completely barred from composing Vedic hymns.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Women scholars (Brahmavadinis) like Lopamudra and Ghosha composed Vedic hymns, making Statement 2 incorrect.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following terms refers to the practice where a childless widow cohabited with her brother-in-law to produce a male heir in Rigvedic society?

opts: Artisans like carpenters (Takshan) and metalworkers enjoyed high social respect and sat in assemblies
Artisans were treated as Shudras and excluded from tribal councils
Metalworking was unknown to the Rigvedic Aryans
Weaving was strictly restricted to male members of the family
practiceQuestions.sol: Artisans like the Takshan (carpenter) were vital for building chariots and weapons, maintaining high status and council participation.

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Goghna' was used in the Rigvedic era to refer to:
opts: An honored guest for whom a cow or ox was slaughtered in hospitality
A criminal who committed cattle theft
A title given to the chief priest during sacrifices
The officer who monitored pasture boundaries
practiceQuestions.sol: Goghna literally means 'one for whom a cow is slain', denoting an honored guest welcomed with peak hospitality.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the status of the 'Shudra' Varna in the Rigvedic period:
1. The Shudras are mentioned throughout the core texts of the early Mandalas.
2. The Shudra category emerged at the end of the period, representing assimilated indigenous populations.
3. The term first appears in the Purusha Sukta hymn in the 10th Mandala.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Shudras are not mentioned in the early Mandalas (2-9), but appear only in the later 10th Mandala's Purusha Sukta.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the status of land ownership in the early Rigvedic period?
opts: Land was communally owned by the clan (Vis/Jana), and individual land titles did not exist
The Rajan owned all lands and rented them to the Vispatis
Individual families possessed rigid title deeds registered by Purohitas
Women inherited agricultural fields while cattle went to sons
practiceQuestions.sol: Rigvedic society was pastoral and semi-nomadic; land was communal and not subject to individual private sales or inheritance.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the early Vedic educational system:
1. It was based on oral transmission without written texts.
2. The system was centralized under the state assembly (Samiti).
3. Only boys were permitted to undergo Vedic education.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Education was oral and family/household centered (early Gurukula). Girls (Brahmavadinis) were initiated into Vedic studies, so Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect.

practiceQuestions.q: The Rigvedic term 'Atka' refers to which of the following?
opts: A golden necklace used as currency
practiceQuestions.sol: The Atka (or Adhivasa) was an outer garment, cloak, or mantle draped over the shoulders by Vedic men and women.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the socio-economic differences between the Aryas and the Dasyus/Dasas in the Rigveda:
1. The Dasyus were described as flat-nosed (Anasa) and of dark complexion.
2. The Dasyus did not perform sacrifices (Akarman) and had different religious practices.
3. The Dasas were completely exterminated and never integrated into Aryan society.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Dasas and Dasyus were defeated but integrated as Shudras/servants rather than being completely exterminated, making Statement 3 false.

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigveda, what was the primary source of metallic tools and weapons denoted by the term 'Ayas'?
practiceQuestions.sol: In early Rigvedic times, 'Ayas' referred to copper or bronze. Iron was discovered later and called 'Krishna-ayas' or 'Shyama-ayas'.

practiceQuestions.q: The gold ornament called 'Niska', which was worn around the neck, also served in Rigvedic times as a:
opts: Medium of exchange and trade value
practiceQuestions.sol: Niska was a gold neck ornament that began to be used as a unit of value or currency in barter transactions.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to social practices, which of the following is TRUE regarding polygamy in Rigvedic society?
opts: Monogamy was the general rule, though polygamy existed among chieftains and nobles
Polygamy was strictly prohibited by customary laws
Polyandry was the dominant form of marriage across all clans
Marriage was temporary and dissolved after five years
practiceQuestions.sol: Monogamy was the standard social norm, but kings and high noble warriors did practice polygamy (multiple wives).

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the status of the 'Grihapati' in Rigvedic family hierarchy:
1. The Grihapati was the master of the household and owned family pastures.
2. The Grihapati represented the family in local assemblies (Sabha).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. The Grihapati (family head) managed the domestic unit and represented it in assemblies.

practiceQuestions.q: Who was the female seer mentioned in the Rigveda as having composed hymns and sponsored sacrifices to secure marital bliss?
practiceQuestions.sol: Vishvavara is one of the celebrated female composers of Rigvedic hymns, alongside Apala and Lopamudra.

practiceQuestions.q: In early Vedic society, the secondary alcoholic beverage 'Sura' was characterized as:
opts: A secular, grain-based liquor popular among commoners but frowned upon by priests
A mountain herb extract used only in Soma sacrifices
A milk-honey mixture offered to deceased ancestors
A purification chemical used by weavers to dye garments
practiceQuestions.sol: Sura was grain liquor consumed during popular celebrations, but frowned upon in religious contexts due to its intoxicating nature.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the position of the father (Kulapa/Grihapati) in Rigvedic family administration?
opts: He had broad patriarchal powers, but could not sell or disinherit his children under customary ethics
He held absolute divine rights of life and death over children without any checks
He was subordinate to the mother in domestic affairs
His authority was shared equally with the eldest daughter of the household
practiceQuestions.sol: Though patriarchal authority was strong, child protection and family ethics restricted extreme abuses like selling children.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the early Vedic diet and agricultural habits:
1. The Rigvedic diet was predominantly vegetarian, heavily centered on dairy products.
2. Barley (Yava) was roasted and mixed with milk or ghee as a common dish (Karambha).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Karambha was a popular dish made of barley flour mixed with ghee or curd.

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic social vocabulary, the word 'Sajana' refers to which group?
opts: Members of the same clan or kinship lineage
practiceQuestions.sol: Sajana represents clansmen or kinsmen who shared common bloodline and fought together in battles.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following games was a highly popular amusement in Rigvedic society but also warned against due to its ruinous effects?
practiceQuestions.sol: Dicing (playing with Aksa/dice) was popular, but Rigvedic hymns (like the Gambler's Lament in Mandala 10) warn against its addictive ruin.

practiceQuestions.q:
Assertion (A): Rigvedic women did not possess independent legal rights to inherit paternal property.
Reason (R): Rigvedic society was patriarchal and focused on patrilineal descent and family integrity.
Codes:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are true. Women held high status but property was held and inherited by males to keep lineage herds intact.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following metal types was referred to by the Rigvedic term 'Krishna-ayas' in the Later Vedic texts?
practiceQuestions.sol: Krishna-ayas (black metal) refers to iron, which only appears in Later Vedic texts. Early Rigvedic used 'Ayas' (bronze/copper).

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to the craftsmen of the Rigvedic era, who was the 'Charmakara'?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Charmakara was a leatherworker who produced shields, bowstrings, reins, and water bags from animal hides.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the status of widows in Rigvedic society:
1. Widow remarriage was legally and socially permitted.
2. The custom of burning widows on the funeral pyre (Sati) was highly prevalent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Widow remarriage was allowed, and Sati was completely absent in the early Rigvedic period (so Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: The Rigvedic division between Aryas and Dasas was primarily based on which parameters?
opts: Rigid hereditary caste lines registered in guilds
Geographical borders divided by the Indus river
The iron technology used in chariot wheels
practiceQuestions.sol: The early division was linguistic (Mridhravac/hostile speech) and ritual (anyavrata/different rites), not based on rigid caste lines.

practiceQuestions.q: What was the term used in the Rigvedic period for girls who chose to remain unmarried and stay at their father's house throughout their lives?
practiceQuestions.sol: Amaju was the term for females who remained unmarried and lived in their parent's home, receiving a share in ancestral maintenance.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding early Vedic social transitions:
1. The migration to the Ganga-Yamuna Doab triggered settled agriculture.
2. The surplus from agriculture led to class division and increased status for ruling groups.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Eastward migration and agriculture led to surplus wealth accumulation by chieftains and priests, creating class divisions.

practiceQuestions.q: In the context of the early Vedic economy, which animal is described as the standard of barter transactions?
practiceQuestions.sol: The cow was the standard unit of value, though horses and gold ornaments were also used.

practiceQuestions.q: The prestigious gold ornament 'Rukma' mentioned in the Rigveda was worn as a:
opts: Breastplate or disc ornament worn on the chest
practiceQuestions.sol: Rukma was a brilliant gold plate or disc ornament worn on the chest, often mentioned in descriptions of gods like Maruts.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Vedic food and drinks:
1. Soma was a drink offered to the gods during sacrifices.
2. Sura was an alcoholic beverage prepared from grains.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Soma was highly sacred (religious), while Sura was secular and popular grain alcohol.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following Rigvedic terms represents a group of families forming a mobile kin group under a leader?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Grama was a mobile camp of kinsmen led by the Gramani.

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Sabhāvati' in the Rigvedic texts demonstrates which aspect of social life?
opts: Women had the right to participate in assembly discussions
The assembly was headed by a female queen
Polygamy was the standard norm of the royal court
Special quarters were reserved for female artisans
practiceQuestions.sol: Sabhāvati proves that women actively participated in and deliberated in the political councils of the early Vedic period.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to the class division in the Later Vedic period, which Rigvedic hymn laid the cosmic justification for the Varna hierarchy?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Purusha Sukta (10th Mandala) justified class hierarchy by linking varnas to the creation from the primeval giant.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the early Vedic crafts:
1. Weaving (spinning and loom work) was primarily performed by women.
2. The carpenter (Takshan) enjoyed a respected status due to chariot-making.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Weaving was a major female craft, and carpenters had high status due to ratha-making.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following represents the correct hierarchical order of social units from the smallest to the largest in Rigvedic society?
practiceQuestions.sol: The order is Kula (family), Grama (clan unit), Vis (clan canton), and Jana (entire tribe).

practiceQuestions.q:
Assertion (A): Rigvedic society was patriarchal but women enjoyed high respect.
Reason (R): Girls received Vedic education, attended assemblies, and child marriage was absent.
Codes:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are true, and the freedom/education of women explains their respected status within the patriarchy.

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic period, the metalworker who worked with copper and bronze was called:
practiceQuestions.sol: The Karmara worked with Ayas (copper/bronze) to manufacture tools and weapons.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following Rigvedic terms represents a female weaver?
practiceQuestions.sol: Vayatri denotes a female weaver in Rigvedic occupational structure.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the non-Aryan tribe called 'Panis':
1. They were rich traders who hoarded cattle herds.
2. They were highly praised by Vedic priests for sponsoring sacrifices.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Panis were rich cattle-owners but were hated by priests because they refused to perform sacrifices (so Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic context, the term 'Amaju' represents:
opts: A woman who chose to remain unmarried throughout her life
A childless widow who remarried her brother-in-law
The head of the local artisan guild
A girl married at an early mature age
practiceQuestions.sol: Amaju refers to a woman who chose lifelong spinsterhood and resided with her parental family.

practiceQuestions.q: The pastoral mobility of the early Vedic people had which political and social consequence?
opts: It prevented the growth of fixed cities and territorial boundaries
It led to the early establishment of empires with written laws
It resulted in the complete absence of family hierarchy
It forced the transition of the entire population to rice agriculture
practiceQuestions.sol: Pastoral nomadism made it difficult to establish sedentary cities or territorial state systems.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following foods was NOT known or consumed by the early Rigvedic people?
practiceQuestions.sol: Rice (Vrihi) was not known in the early Sapta-Sindhu phase; it appears in Later Vedic texts as clans moved to the wetter Ganga valley.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to Rigvedic ornaments, the ornament 'Rukma' was traditionally made of:
practiceQuestions.sol: Rukma was a brilliant gold chest-piece ornament.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of 'Gramani' in Rigvedic social layout:
1. The Gramani led the mobile family clusters (Grama) during migrations.
2. The Gramani was the head priest who conducted domestic rituals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. The Gramani was a village/clan head who led them in migrations and military raids, not a priest.

practiceQuestions.q: The system of weregild or blood-money compensation for murder in Rigvedic justice was called:
practiceQuestions.sol: Vairadeya was the system of weregild where murder was compensated in cows to prevent blood feuds.

practiceQuestions.q: Which assembly is described in the Rigveda as a place for social entertainment, dicing, and music alongside political debates?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Sabha was not only a political council but also a center of social life, dicing, music, and gatherings.

mockTestQuestions.q: In early Vedic society, who was the master of the household who held patriarchal authority over the family?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Grihapati (or Kulapa) was the male head of the patriarchal family unit (Kula/Griha).

mockTestQuestions.q: The four-fold Varna system appears for the first time in which part of the Rigvedic corpus?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Purusha Sukta of Mandala 10 first describes the creation of the four Varnas from the cosmic giant's body.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which term in the Rigveda is used to describe a woman eligible to sit and participate in assembly discussions?
mockTestQuestions.sol: A Sabhāvati was a woman who had the right to sit and participate in the Sabha assembly.

mockTestQuestions.q: What was the principal grain cultivated by the early Indo-Aryans in the Sapta-Sindhu region?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Yava (barley) was the primary crop; rice (Vrihi) was introduced in Later Vedic times.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which artisan group was held in high respect due to their role in building battle chariots (Rathas)?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Carpenters (Takshan) held a highly respected administrative and social position because of chariot-crafting.

mockTestQuestions.q: The term 'Aghnya' in the Rigveda, applied to cows, literally means:
mockTestQuestions.sol: Aghnya literally means 'not to be killed/slain', denoting the sacred and economic value of the cow.

mockTestQuestions.q: What was the nature of the sacred plant beverage 'Soma' in Rigvedic rituals?
opts: It was a mountain-plant beverage offered to the gods and consumed in sacrifices
It was a grain-brewed secular alcohol consumed in public festivals
It was a dairy product used as currency in barter transactions
It was a dye used by weavers to color wool garments
mockTestQuestions.sol: Soma was a highly sacred plant beverage offered to gods (especially Indra) to gain vitality.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which social custom was completely absent in the early Rigvedic societal setup?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Sati (widow burning) and child marriage were completely absent in the early Vedic societal setup.

mockTestQuestions.q: The hierarchical ascending order of social units in early Vedic times is:
mockTestQuestions.sol: The correct ascending order is Kula (family), Grama (clan unit), Vis (clan subdivision), and Jana (tribe).

mockTestQuestions.q: In Rigvedic justice, what was the weregild (blood-money compensation) system called?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Vairadeya was the system of weregild where murder was compensated in cows to resolve disputes.
